etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English bold, bolde, bald, beald, from Old English bald, beald (“bold, brave, confident, strong, of good courage, presumptuous, impudent”), from Proto-West Germanic *balþ, from Proto-Germanic *balþaz (“strong, bold”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel-, *bʰlē- (“to bloat, swell, bubble”).

Cognate with Dutch boud (“bold, courageous, fearless”), Middle High German balt (“bold”) (whence German bald (“soon”)), Swedish båld (“bold, dauntless”). Perhaps related to Albanian ballë (“forehead”) and Old Prussian balo (“forehead”). For semantic development compare Italian affrontare (“to face, to deal with”), sfrontato (“bold, daring, insolent”), both from Latin frons (“forehead”).

quote.citation: 1918, W[illiam] B[abington] Maxwell, chapter XXII, in The Mirror and the Lamp, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: Not unnaturally, “Auntie” took this communication in bad part. Thus outraged, she showed herself to be a bold as well as a furious virago. Next day she found her way to their lodgings and tried to recover her ward by the hair of the head.

quote.citation: 2005, Plato, translated by Lesley Brown, Sophist, page 239c:
quote.text: It would be extraordinarily bold of me to give it a try after seeing what has happened to you.

definitions.definition: (typography, of typefaces) Having thicker strokes than the ordinary form of the typeface.

quote.citation: 1748, [David Hume], “Essay I. On the different Species of Philosophy.”, in Philosophical Essays Concerning Human Understanding, London:  […]  A[ndrew] Millar, […], →OCLC, part I, page 18:
quote.text: […]  even the boldeſt and moſt affirmative Philoſophy, which has ever attempted to impoſe its crude Dictates and Principles on Mankind.

quote.citation: 1808, William Bernard Cooke, A New Picture of the Isle of Wight, page 144:
quote.text: The grounds descend with a bold slope to the water's edge, and rise finely upwards above the mansion, abounding with fine trees, and ornamented by a range of building at a distance, in a corresponding style  […]

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English bolden, balden, from Old English baldian, bealdian, from Proto-Germanic *balþōną, related to *balþaz (see above). Cognate with Old High German irbaldōn (“to become bold, dare”).

definitions.definition: (transitive, informal) To make (a font or some text) bold.
(transitive, obsolete) To make bold or daring.[1]

quote.citation: c. 1603–1606 (date written), [William Shakespeare],  […]  His True Chronicle Historie of the Life and Death of King Lear and His Three Daughters. […] (First Quarto), London:  […]  Nathaniel Butter, […], published 1608, →OCLC, [Act V, scene i]:
quote.text: […]  for this buſines,It touches vs, as France inuades our landNot bolds the King, with others whome I feare,Moſt iuſt and heauy cauſes make oppoſe.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, obsolete) To become bold or brave.[1]

etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English bold, from Old English bold, blod, bolt, botl (“house, dwelling-place, mansion, hall, castle, temple”), from Proto-Germanic *budlą, *buþlą (“house, dwelling”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰew- (“to grow, wax, swell”) or *bʰuH-.

Cognate with Old Frisian bold (“house”) (whence North Frisian bol, boel, bøl (“house”)), North Frisian bodel, budel (“property, inheritance”), Middle Low German būdel (“property, real estate”). Related to build.
